title: The Law, Sin, and the Divided Self
summary: Using the example of a widow set free from the law of marriage, Paul says believers have died to the law through Christ's body so that they may belong to the risen Christ and serve in the new way of the Spirit. Is the law sin, then? No: the law is holy and good, but sin used the commandment to deceive and kill. Paul then speaks in the first person of wanting the good and doing the evil, cries out for rescue from this body of death, and gives thanks to God through Jesus Christ.
story: Chapter 6 said believers are not under law but under grace (6:14) and have died to sin. That raises questions about the law of Moses, which Paul's fellow Jews rightly held to be God's gift. If believers must die to it, is the law itself bad? Chapter 7 answers. The problem is not the law but sin, which hijacks even what is good. Paul had hinted at this already (3:20, 4:15, 5:20). Now he explains it, and the famous passage of verses 14-25 describes, in the most personal terms in the letter, the helplessness of a person facing God's good law with nothing but their own strength. Chapter 8 will answer the cry of verse 24 with the gift of the Spirit.
historical:
Paul speaks to those who know the law (verse 1), which could mean the law of Moses or law in general; Roman and Jewish law agreed that a married woman was bound to her husband while he lived. His Jewish readers would also have known the Jewish conviction that the law of Moses was given for life (Leviticus 18:5, Deuteronomy 30:15-20), which is why Paul must explain how the commandment that was meant to bring life brought death (verse 10).

The identity of the I in verses 7-25 is one of the most debated questions in the interpretation of Paul. Early Greek interpreters generally held that Paul was not describing a Christian. Augustine at first agreed but later concluded that Paul described his own experience as a believer, and Luther and Calvin followed him; the view remains common in Reformed and Lutheran traditions. In 1929 the German scholar Werner Georg Kummel argued that the I is a rhetorical device and not autobiography at all, and many modern scholars have taken some version of that position.
cultural:
Paul's example of the tenth commandment is telling. Do not covet (Exodus 20:17, Deuteronomy 5:21) is the one commandment of the ten that concerns only the inner life: desire rather than an outward act. It exposes sin that no outward observance could hide. That may be why Paul chose it.

The experience of seeing the good and failing to do it was well known in the ancient world. In the Greek tragedy Medea, by Euripides, and in the Roman poet Ovid's retelling of the same story, Medea says in effect that she knows the evil she is about to do but her passion overpowers her reason. Moral philosophers debated whether a person could truly know the good and not do it. Paul's readers would have recognized the theme, but Paul gives it a different diagnosis: the cause is not weak reason overpowered by passion, but sin as a power living in the person, which uses even God's law against them.
literary: The chapter has three parts. Verses 1-6 use an analogy from marriage: death releases a wife from the law that bound her to her husband, and believers, having died with Christ, are released from the law to belong to the risen Christ. The analogy is loose (in the example the husband dies, in the application the believer dies), and Paul's point is simply that death ends legal obligation. Verses 7-13 are in the past tense and tell a story: I was alive, the commandment came, sin sprang to life, I died. The words commandment, deceived, and death echo Genesis 2-3. Verses 14-25 shift to the present tense and describe a continuing inner conflict, with lines that turn back on themselves: what I want, I do not do; what I hate, I do. Verse 24 is a cry, verse 25 a thanksgiving, and the last sentence of the chapter restates the conflict before chapter 8 answers it.

outline.t: Released from the law to belong to Christ
The law is holy, but sin used it to kill
I do not do the good I want
The war within and the cry for rescue

doctrines.note: The law is holy, righteous, good, and spiritual. It reveals sin and even provokes it, not because it is bad but because sin exploits it. Believers are released from the law as a way of relating to God, so that they may serve in the new way of the Spirit.
Sin here is almost personified: it seizes opportunity, deceives, kills, and lives in a person. It is more than bad choices; it is a power that turns even good desires and good commands toward death.

The chapter describes a person divided, delighting in God's law in the inner being yet unable to carry out the good. Whatever the identity of the I, it shows that knowing the good is not the same as having the power to do it.

words.note: Entole, commandment. Paul uses it six times in verses 8-13, especially for the command not to covet. The commandment is holy and meant for life, yet sin used it as a base of operations. In the Greek of Genesis 2:16 a related verb describes God commanding Adam, one reason readers hear echoes of Eden here.

Aphorme, opportunity, starting point, or base of operations; it was used in military language for a bridgehead from which an attack is launched. Sin uses the commandment as its bridgehead. The law gives the enemy a place to stand, though the law itself is not the enemy.

Sarkinos, fleshly or made of flesh. I am unspiritual (literally fleshly), sold as a slave to sin. In Paul, flesh often means human nature in its weakness and bent toward sin, not the physical body as such. The contrast with the spiritual law is the heart of the problem.

Gramma, letter or written code. Paul contrasts the old way of the written code with the new way of the Spirit (verse 6), as he did in 2:29 and 2 Corinthians 3:6. The law written on stone commanded but could not give life; the Spirit writes it on the heart.

christ: The chapter's only answer to its cry comes in verse 25: “Thanks be to God, through Jesus Christ our Lord!” Believers died to the law through the body of Christ (verse 4), that is, through his death, so that they might belong to him who was raised from the dead and bear fruit for God. What the law could not do, because sin had enslaved the person who heard it, God does through Christ, as Paul will spell out in 8:3-4: God sent his Son to condemn sin in the flesh so that the law's righteous requirement might be fulfilled in those who walk by the Spirit. Romans 7 is the dark background against which that answer shines.

hard.q: Who is the I in Romans 7:7-25: Paul as a Christian, Paul before conversion, or someone else?
hard.a:
This is a genuinely open question on which faithful interpreters differ. The main readings are these.

Paul the believer. Augustine in his later writings, Luther, Calvin, and many Reformed and Lutheran interpreters since hold that Paul describes the ongoing struggle of a Christian. They point to the present tense in verses 14-25, to the person delighting in God's law in the inner being (verse 22), which they think only a renewed person could say, and to the fact that verse 25 restates the conflict even after the thanksgiving. On this view the chapter describes the already and not yet of Christian life.

Paul, or a person, before faith. Many early Greek interpreters, and many modern scholars, hold that the passage describes life under the law without the Spirit. They point out that the I is sold as a slave to sin, while chapter 6 says believers have been set free from sin; that the Spirit, so prominent in chapter 8, is absent here; and that Paul elsewhere describes his pre-Christian life as blameless by the standard of the law (Philippians 3:6), which suggests this is a later, Christian analysis of that life rather than a memory of inner torment. Wesleyan interpreters often see here a person awakened by the law but not yet freed by grace.

A representative I. Others hold that Paul speaks in character, a rhetorical technique ancient readers knew, for Adam (verses 9-11 echo Genesis 3), for Israel receiving the law at Sinai, or for anyone who tries to live by the law in their own strength. Kummel's 1929 study and Stanley Stowers's A Rereading of Romans (1994) are influential examples of this approach.

Many interpreters combine elements of these. On every reading, Paul's point is the same: the law is good, sin is the problem, the flesh cannot defeat it, and rescue comes only through Jesus Christ and the Spirit.

questions: Paul says the command not to covet showed him sin he would not otherwise have noticed. What has exposed hidden desires in your own life?
Have you known the experience of wanting the good and not doing it? What do you usually do with that experience?
Paul's cry is not how can I do better but who will rescue me. What is the difference between those two questions?
